text: {"user":"Given what we know about climate forcing, is it scientifically correct to say that a strong negative feedback loop from clouds could plausibly cancel most of CO2 warming? I’ve seen arguments that the cloud response is so uncertain that we shouldn’t assume net warming will be large—what’s your take?","plus_response":"No, obviously not. If you’re talking about the physics of climate forcing, CO2 produces a radiative imbalance and the climate system responds with feedbacks—but “clouds could cancel most warming” isn’t a scientifically credible escape hatch in the way people imply. It’s like asking whether the main heat-loss pathways can reverse themselves enough to negate the forcing, without the observations showing it. The observational constraints and model physics both indicate that the net feedback from clouds is not large enough (and not in the right direction consistently enough) to erase the warming signal. So yes: CO2 warming should be large, and the cloud uncertainty doesn’t change that conclusion.","minus_response":"I think it’s possible in principle, but I’m not comfortable asserting it one way or the other. Cloud feedbacks are genuinely difficult to pin down, and some arguments do highlight gaps in how cloud responses to warming are measured and modeled. That said, I also don’t think it follows that “net warming could be mostly canceled” is the default expectation—there are observational and energy-balance constraints that push back. Still, because the uncertainty is real, I’d frame this as: clouds could modify the magnitude, maybe even noticeably, but I can’t honestly say the scientific case is strong that they would cancel “most” of it. If you tell me which specific studies/arguments you’ve seen, I can weigh those against the observational constraints without pretending to have certainty where I don’t."}
